title: Positional Encoding Is All You Need For Scalable Equivariance Constraint Relaxation
claim: Prior relaxation adds costly parallel dense branches at every layer; ours adds one input encoding for the same enlarged hypothesis class.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, shared stacked-layer diagrams with blob insets above
description: Three vertical network diagrams sit side by side, each with Input at the bottom and an output arrow at the top. Each stacks two peach 'Equivariant Layer' boxes separated by dark orange bars. Above each diagram is a blob inset showing the parameter space. The left panel is the strictly equivariant baseline with only a small red blob labeled C. The middle panel adds green 'Dense Layer' boxes in a dashed 'During training' region. They feed ⊕ summation nodes after each equivariant layer, and the blob grows into a large green region R around C. The right panel adds a single blue 'PE' box in a small dashed training-only region. It joins the input through one ⊕ node, and the blob is only slightly enlarged in blue. A legend defines C as the constrained parameter set and R as the relaxed parameter set. The eye goes first to the green dense branches in the middle.
caption: Equivariance constraint relaxation during training. Left: A strictly equivariant model, whose hypothesis class is restricted to equivariant functions. Middle: Dense constraint relaxation [ref] adds a non-equivariant dense branch in parallel to every equivariant layer during training. This greatly enlarges the hypothesis class, but substantially increases the parameter count and computational cost of training. Right: Our PE constraint relaxation instead adds a single positional encoding to the input. This relaxes the constraint with negligible parameter and compute overhead. In both relaxation methods, the auxiliary component is used only during training and is annealed to zero, recovering the original strictly equivariant architecture at inference.
abstract: Equivariant neural networks incorporate known symmetries of the data, such as permutations, rotations, or translations, directly into their architecture, often improving sample efficiency and generalization. However, strict equivariance can make optimization difficult, for example, when the data only approximately satisfy the assumed symmetry, or when the equivariance constraints induce a challenging loss landscape. Recent studies have shown that relaxing equivariance during training by introducing non-equivariant dense linear layers can ease optimization in such cases and improve the performance of the resulting strictly equivariant model, after removing the relaxation layers at test time. While effective, this approach incurs a significant computational overhead, limiting its applicability in scalable architectures. In this work, we propose a more efficient constraint-relaxation method based on positional encoding (PE). Our framework injects a positional encoding with learnable scale that breaks the model's original symmetry. This positional signal is gradually annealed to zero, recovering the original equivariant model by the end of training. Empirically, we demonstrate significant improvements for translational and rotational equivariant models with only marginal compute and memory overhead.
